paper_title: SpatialArena: Where Do Geometric Foundation Models Stand?

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: 3D perception is shifting from task-specific pipelines to geometric foundation models: monocular depth networks, feed-forward 3D/4D reconstruction models, and vision--language models that predict geometry. However, their progress cannot be measured reliably. Published numbers are not comparable, because every paper samples frames, sets resolutions, and selects test splits differently. They are not robust because the alignment required for every up-to-scale prediction can outweigh the gap between models: fitting depth in the wrong space nearly triples its error, and standard trajectory alignment understates the error of failing methods by up to $2.6\times$. And they rarely cover long recordings, dynamic scenes, or aerial views. We present SpatialArena, an open arena that scores geometric models with the same metrics and rules, with robust and deterministic alignment. SpatialArena spans five tasks, from monocular depth to SLAM. It covers 23 public datasets with 418,929 images across indoor, outdoor, aerial, object-centric, and dynamic scenes, together with Spatial Arena, our own captures with accurate poses and depth. Evaluating 52 models, we find that single-image depth is close to saturation on public benchmarks but not on large, uncontrolled scenes, and that progress now comes from consistency across frames and views, where feed-forward 3D/4D models match or surpass monocular specialists and overtake video depth models. The benchmark, toolbox, and leaderboard will be publicly released.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Perceiving the 3D world from images is one of the oldest goals of computer vision, and it is undergoing the shift that natural language processing went through few years ago. Depth, camera pose, and scene geometry, traditionally estimated by separate hand-engineered pipelines [58, 71, 72], are now predicted by large networks trained on massive data: monocular depth models generalize to unseen scenes without further finetuning [6, 44, 93, 102], feed-forward 3D/4D models predict cameras, depth, and point maps for thousands of frames in one pass [15, 55, 88, 91, 94, 95], and visionlanguage models begin to predict metric geometry [12, 14, 107]. These geometric foundation models raise questions beyond any single task. Will general models absorb the specialized ones, as large language models (LLMs) did in NLP? Where do 1 SpatialArena: Where Do Geometric Foundation Models Stand? Figure 1. Overview of the SpatialArena benchmark. (a) SpatialArena against existing geometry benchmarks along six axes, each normalized by its largest value (sequence length in log frames); E3D-Bench dataset counts are lower bound. (b) Datasets, models, and longest sequence of each benchmark. (c) Score of eight leading models on each dataset; marks datasets excluded from the ranking. No model leads on every dataset. (d) Evaluated models by family. (e) Scenes of our Spatial Arena dataset, which feeds all five tasks. improvements actually come from? And is the field converging toward models that understand 3D geometry, or toward models that fit few test sets? Answering them requires measurement. Shared benchmarks have shaped both vision and language: ImageNet [23] made progress in recognition visible and comparable, and holistic evaluations and open arenas [19, 54] track how LLMs evolve across many abilities at once. Geometric foundation models have no such common ground, and three problems make their results hard to compare. First, every work evaluates with its own tools. Frame sampling, input resolution, test splits, and evaluation code differ from paper to paper [44, 55, 91], so reported gap between two models may come from evaluation rather than from the models. Second, metric computation is neither consistent nor robust. Most models predict geometry up to scale, so every score passes through an alignment to the ground truth, and that alignment can matter more than the model. Fitting disparity model in depth space nearly triples its AbsRel, least-squares fit raises the AbsRel of strong multi-view models by more than 50% (Sec. D), and the closed-form fit on camera centers used for trajectories [30, 84] understates the error of failing methods by up to 2.6 (Sec. D). Third, coverage is partial. Most papers report results on subset of public datasets, rarely on the regimes that matter in practice: dynamic scenes, aerial views, weakly textured objects, or recordings of thousands of frames. Some test scenes are even part of the evaluated models training data (Sec. A). As result, it is unclear how far geometric foundation models have actually come, and in which direction. We argue that the field needs an arena: an open platform where geometric models are evaluated with the same metrics, under the same rules. SpatialArena is built on three principles. Fairness. One evaluation suite scores every model from its outputs using the same inputs, alignment, and metrics, and excludes the datasets models were trained on from the ranking. Robust measurement. Depth is aligned by robust fit in each models native output space on pixels chosen by the ground truth alone, and trajectories by pose-aware, outlier-robust similarity estimator. Breadth. SpatialArena spans five tasks, from monocular and video depth 2 SpatialArena: Where Do Geometric Foundation Models Stand? to multi-view reconstruction, structure from motion, and SLAM on recordings of nearly 19k frames, on 23 public datasets of indoor, outdoor, aerial, object-centric, static, and dynamic scenes and on Spatial Arena, 30 new large-scale scenes captured with handheld LiDAR and three-camera rig, with accurate camera poses and depth. We evaluate 52 depth, feed-forward 3D/4D, long-sequence SLAM, and open and commercial visionlanguage models, and three findings stand out (Sec. 4). First, single-image depth is close to saturation on the public benchmarks: the best monocular AbsRel there improved only from 5.5% to 4.9% in two years, whereas on our large, uncontrolled captures the errors are three to four times higher; the remaining headroom lies in fine accuracy and in such scenes. Second, general models are absorbing specialized ones: feed-forward 3D/4D models match the monocular specialists on public data, surpass them once our captures are scored, and, on video depth, halve the error of the best dedicated model. Third, visionlanguage models improve fastest on single-image depth but remain far behind, lacking metric precision and consistency across frames. No model leads on every dataset, so the field has not yet converged on one model of 3D structure. In summary, our contributions are: SpatialArena, an open arena that evaluates geometric foundation models on five tasks, 23 public datasets, and our captures under one protocol; robust, deterministic alignment for depth and trajectories, with comparison of six depth alignments and controlled study showing that the standard trajectory alignment hides failures; an evaluation of 52 models across specialist, feed-forward, and visionlanguage families that traces how geometric foundation models are evolving.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Depth foundation models. Affine-invariant training on mixed data [68, 69] made monocular depth zero-shot. Later work adds unlabeled and synthetic data [101, 102], diffusion priors [34, 44], metric depth, cameras, or point maps [6, 37, 67, 92, 93], and arbitrary output resolution [106], mostly on self-supervised backbones [61]; video models add temporal consistency [16, 38, 108]. Each reports results under its own alignment and test split [27]. Feed-forward multi-view geometry. DUSt3R [94] and MASt3R [51] regress point maps from uncalibrated image pairs, and successors scale to many views with spatial memory [11, 86, 91] or single forward pass [99]. VGGT [88] predicts cameras, depth, and point maps from hundreds of frames, and was refined for permutation equivariance [95], depthray outputs [55], accuracy and metric scale [9, 87, 89], efficiency [18, 76], robustness [31], and semantics [52, 110]; others accept cameras or depth as priors [40, 46, 66]. They now drive SfM [25] and SLAM [56, 59], competing with classical pipelines [58, 63, 71, 72, 83], and reach thousands of frames through chunk alignment [24, 96], test-time training [41], compact memories [15, 32, 109], or local pose regression [97], each evaluated on its own sequences and trajectory alignment. Geometry from general-purpose models. Visionlanguage models answer spatial questions [14, 100] or predict metric depth [12, 82, 107], and video generators are repurposed as geometry estimators [90]. Probing studies ask how much 3D structure such models encode [4, 7]. Commercial VLMs, such as Claude [2], GPT [60], and Gemini [29], are available only through APIs and do not disclose their training data. Neither open nor commercial models are routinely evaluated alongside dedicated 3D models. Benchmarks. Most papers reuse the protocols of Marigold [44], π3 [95], and DA3-BENCH [55], with differing sampling, resolution, and alignment, and trajectories rely on an Umeyama fit on camera centers [30, 84]. RobustMVD [74] evaluates multi-view depth, GeoBench [27] retrains monocular models under controlled settings, and E3D-Bench [20] evaluates 16 geometric foundation models. Concurrent SpatialBench [65] evaluates 41 model variants on 19 datasets, and UAVFF3D [103] targets UAV imagery. 3 SpatialArena: Where Do Geometric Foundation Models Stand? Figure 2. Datasets of SpatialArena. (a) Evaluation cases by environment, static or dynamic scenes, and scene type (inner rings), and per dataset, stacked by task. (b) Unique images per dataset; the 23 public datasets hold 418,929 images. (c) Conditions each dataset tests and the tasks that use it. All five tasks test indoor and outdoor scenes, whereas aerial views, internet photos, and recordings of more than 10k frames are tested by one task each. Spatial Arena adds large-scale scenes with accurate poses and depth to all five tasks.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: SpatialArena evaluates spatial foundation models on five geometric tasks. We first define the tasks and input tracks (Sec. 3.1), then introduce the Spatial Arena dataset (Sec. 3.2) and the depth and trajectory alignment shared by all tasks (Sec. 3.3). We then summarize the datasets and metrics of each task (Sec. 3.4) and the evaluated models (Sec. 3.5). The data leakage audit is described in Sec. A.

sections.title: 3.2 Spatial Arena Dataset
sections.content: Data capture. Public benchmarks rarely provide metric ground truth for large, uncontrolled scenes captured by handheld devices. We therefore collect Spatial Arena with handheld scanner that records LiDAR point clouds and three synchronized cameras; the front camera faces the direction of walking, and the two side cameras look up and sideways. The benchmark uses 30 scenes, 13 indoor and 17 outdoor: museum halls, station concourses, library, an office floor, and stairwell; streets, alleys, gardens, markets, plazas, and monuments  (Fig. 3)  . Walks range from 18 to over 1 km, and LiDAR depth from below 1 to over 100 m. In total, Spatial Arena contributes 32,655 unique images, selected per task as described in Sec. A. Processing. The final LiDAR points and camera poses are obtained by LiDAR SLAM and post-processed by iterative global bundle adjustment [71]. Projecting the LiDAR map into every camera with z-buffer gives sparse metric depth, and SAM 3.1 [13] masks people, vehicles, and sky, which are excluded from the valid pixels. To densify the sparse depth, we fit 3D Gaussian Splats (3DGS) [47] to each scene, supervised by LiDAR depth and regularized by depthnormal and multi-view geometric consistency, and render dense depths for images as pseudo-labels; the projected LiDAR depth remains the sparse metric reference. We validate every rendered depth map against the sparse LiDAR depth: over all MonoDepth and VideoDepth frames, 98.3% and 98.2% of the LiDAR pixels agree within 25% (AbsRel 0.036 and 0.030). Since LiDAR has no returns where the rendering fails most often, e.g., near-camera floaters, reflections, and weakly textured surfaces, MonoDepth also selects its images automatically: it keeps only images whose render PSNR exceeds the scene median, so ground truth comes from well-reconstructed views, and samples 10% of each scenes 5 SpatialArena: Where Do Geometric Foundation Models Stand? images spread over time. Finally, every depth frame is checked manually next to its LiDAR and dense depth; frames with depth artifacts are removed from MonoDepth or left unscored in VideoDepth.

sections.title: 3.3 Geometry Alignment
sections.content: Most methods predict geometry only up to an unknown scale, and depth also up to an unknown shift, so every metric is computed after aligning the prediction to the ground truth: one depth alignment for both depth tasks and one trajectory alignment for all pose-based metrics.

sections.title: 3.3.1 Depth Alignment
sections.content: Depth alignment estimates an unknown scale and shift between prediction and ground-truth depth. Models predict in different spaces, i.e., affine-invariant disparity [34, 69], affine-invariant depth [44], or depth up to scale [55, 88], and existing protocols align them differently: by least squares in depth [44] or by ℓ1 with fixed number of gradient steps [91, 95], some only on pixels where the prediction is valid. These choices are not neutral: on identical predictions (Sec. D), least squares in depth raises the AbsRel of VGGT-Ω and DA3-G by 5559% over robust fit, and depth-space fit nearly triples the AbsRel of Lotus-D. We therefore align every model with the same robust, deterministic estimator on pixels chosen by the ground truth alone, and fit it in the space in which the model predicts: in depth for depth outputs and in inverse depth for disparity outputs. Solver. We minimize Eq. (2) with LevenbergMarquardt in three steps. Because no subset of frames is exactly right under smooth drift, we then refit on all frames by iteratively reweighted least squares with Cauchy weights on the normalized residuals; gross errors keep near-zero weight, the result no longer depends on the RANSAC seed, and on clean data it is as precise as least-squares fit. Finally, if the scale collapses toward zero, which happens only for trajectories that fail outright, we fall back to center-only fit and flag the case. Details are in Sec. D.

sections.title: 3.5 Evaluated Models
sections.content: We evaluate 52 models in five families (Tab. 2). Feed-forward 3D/4D models predict cameras, depth, and point maps; they enter the depth, MVRecon, and SfM tasks, and most of them also SLAM; four of them also accept geometric priors and run the rgbc or rgbd tracks. Monocular depth models, both affine-invariant and metric, enter MonoDepth. Video generative models are built on video diffusion or generation backbones and predict video depth, camera poses, or both. Long-sequence and SLAM systems chunk, stream, or compress input to process thousands of frames and enter SLAM only. Finally, visionlanguage models are queried for depth, which places them on the same scale as dedicated geometry models; besides open models, we query three commercial models (Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra, and Gemini 4 Argon) through APIs on MonoDepth. Variants of models, such as the depth and pose variants of GenCeption, count as separate models. We list the input resolution and preprocessing of every model in Sec. D.3.1.

Do newer models perform better? Figure 4 and the VideoDepth plot in Fig. 9 answer this for the two depth tasks, and the answer differs between model families. On MonoDepth, the depth specialists have stalled: their fitted trend falls by 2.8 points per year, and the best of them has improved its AbsRel only from 12.3% (MoGe, 2024) to 11.6% (MoGe-3, 2026). The 3D/4D models rise by 8.4 points per year, and since mid-2025 the best of them has been more accurate than every depth specialist evaluated on all datasets (π3-X, 11.4%; VGGT-Ω, 10.8%). Their advantage comes from Spatial Arena, the only MonoDepth dataset on which the 3D/4D models are clearly more accurate than the specialists (Sec. 5.1); on the public datasets alone, the two families rise by only 1.92.8 points per year and remain on par (Sec. B.3). On VideoDepth, which requires depth that is consistent across frames, the 3D/4D models improve by 28.4 points per year; their best AbsRel fell from 45% (DUSt3R) to 6.5% (VGGT-Ω) in two and half years and has been below that of the best video depth model (GenCeption-Depth, 14.0%) since mid-2025, while depth models improve by 8.7 points per year. VLMs improve fastest on MonoDepth (31.5 points per year) from low base, but on VideoDepth more slowly than the 3D/4D models (14.3), and they still trail the other two families on both tasks. Progress comes mainly from multi-view consistency rather than from single-image accuracy; MVRecon, SfM, and SLAM show the same rise for 3D/4D models (Figs. 9 and 10). Key findings and outlook. We summarize the results along three axes; Sec. 5 discusses each in depth, with the failure cases we observed. (1) Generalizability. General models are absorbing specialized ones: the feed-forward 3D/4D models enter all five tasks, lead MonoDepth once Spatial Arena is scored, lead VideoDepth, and still rise steeply on MVRecon (24.7 points per year) and SLAM (25.5). No model, however, generalizes across all data. The dataset leaders differ even among the top-ranked models (Fig. 1(c)); on the seven ranked MVRecon datasets, six different models have the best F-score. Large, uncontrolled scenes, rather than more of the existing test sets, are where generalization still has to be won. (2) Robustness. No feed-forward model runs the large SLAM range on its own, and the long-sequence systems often fail: ZipMap runs out of GPU memory on every Oxford Spires and VBR sequence, and Scal3R runs out of memory on six of the seven VBR sequences. The range is led by Pi-Long, which chunks the input of feed-forward model. Bounded-memory inference and failure detection, more than further gains on short clips, are what long-sequence models need next. (3) Accuracy. Coarse accuracy is saturated on the public datasets, but fine accuracy is not. There, the best depth model reaches δ1.25 of 96%, gaining under one point per year, but δ1.03 of only 62%; with Spatial Arena scored, the two fall to 87% and 46% (MoGe-3). For VLMs, accuracy is the main bottleneck. sections.title: 5 Discussion
sections.content: The central finding of our evaluation is that models which are accurate on the public benchmarks fail in systematic ways on large, uncontrolled scenes. In this section, we analyze why, along the three axes of Sec. 4: generality (Sec. 5.1), robustness (Sec. 5.2), and accuracy (Sec. 5.3). We then summarize the strengths and weaknesses of each model family (Sec. 5.4) and their implications for future work (Sec. 5.5). Throughout, ρ denotes Spearmans rank correlation, and public denotes models mean over the ranked public datasets of task, which exclude ScanNet++ and Spring (Sec. A).

sections.title: 5.1 Generality
sections.content: Across tasks. Single-image accuracy is poor predictor of multi-view performance. The task scores are strongly correlated among VideoDepth and the multi-view tasks (ρ = 0.88 between VideoDepth and MVRecon, 0.77 between VideoDepth and SLAM, and 0.74 between MVRecon and SLAM), but only weakly between MonoDepth and the pose-dependent tasks (0.52 with SfM, 0.47 with SLAM); DA3-G, for instance, leads MVRecon but ranks eighth in MonoDepth. We attribute this to the different cues that the tasks reward. single image can only be resolved through learned priors about scene layout, whereas consistent depth and poses across views require correspondence, which the multi-view models learn and the monocular ones do not. What makes Spatial Arena difficult. Figure 7 shows how Spatial Arena differs from the public datasets. First, its viewpoints are unusual. The front camera looks along the walking direction and is pitched down by 12 SpatialArena: Where Do Geometric Foundation Models Stand? Figure 7. What makes Spatial Arena difficult. (a) Images from 14 scenes, taken by the front camera (upright views along the walking direction) and the two side cameras (rolled views looking up and sideways): dim museum halls with specular floors, tiled underground platform, close-ups of floors and signs, graffiti, foliage, stairs, and facades seen from below. (b) Depth range within one image (d95/d5 of the valid ground truth; box: quartiles, whiskers: 10th and 90th percentiles) on the 1,688 Spatial Arena MonoDepth images and sample of the real public MonoDepth datasets (Marigold suite without ETH3D). (c) Absolute camera roll of the same images, from the ground-truth poses (world is vertical): the front camera is nearly upright (median 5), whereas the side cameras are rolled by median of 50. (d) Mean MonoDepth AbsRel of four models in bins of camera roll. median of 25, but the two side cameras look up and sideways and are rolled by median of 50 (10th to 90th percentile, 2665; Fig. 7(c)), so that the horizon runs diagonally through the image and facades, ceilings, and sky fill large parts of the view. The public datasets consist almost entirely of upright images taken by person, robot, or car. Second, single image spans wide range of depth: the median ratio between the 95th and 5th percentile of ground-truth depth is 10 on Spatial Arena and reaches 29 at the 90th percentile, against 2.14.4 on HAMMER, iBims-1, the Marigold suite, and AerialMetric (Fig. 7(b)). typical side view contains wall or floor within meter and facade tens of meters away. Third, the camera moves fast relative to the frame rate: on the short SLAM range, it moves 0.55 between input frames, against 0.050.10 on TUM RGB-D and 7-Scenes. Fourth, the scenes vary in content and appearance (Fig. 7(a)): dim museum halls with specular floors and glass cases, tiled underground platform, graffiti and foliage, stairs, and crowded markets, all captured with 90 horizontal field of view. Why models fail on Spatial Arena: MonoDepth. These properties, rather than the scale of the scenes alone, explain most of the drop in accuracy (Tab. 5). To show this, we analyze the stored predictions of each task per image, per pixel, or per image pair, without re-running any model. In MonoDepth, we analyze ten models (VGGT-Ω, π3-X, AMB3R, MoGe-3, UniDepthV2, Depth Pro, DA3-G, VGGT, DUSt3R, and SenseNova-Vision). The clearest evidence is the camera roll. Within the same scenes, the models are about 13 SpatialArena: Where Do Geometric Foundation Models Stand? Figure 8. Why models fail on Spatial Arena, beyond MonoDepth. (a) VideoDepth AbsRel of the Spatial Arena pixels in bins of ground-truth depth (every fourth frame of all 15 clips, with each models sequence alignment). (b) Mean VideoDepth AbsRel on the six front-camera and nine side-camera Spatial Arena clips, for the 15 models without auxiliary inputs that cover all clips. (c) SfM AUC@5 on the seven Spatial Arena scenes, computed separately for image pairs from two front images, from front and side image, from the same side camera, and from different side cameras. (d) Drift of every model on every short-range SLAM sequence (7-Scenes, TUM RGB-D, Oxford Spires, and Spatial Arena) against the ground-truth path length per input frame. (e) Drift on every long-range sequence (7-Scenes, TUM RGB-D, and the two Spatial Arena walks, shaded) against the path length. (f) Drift of four long-sequence systems on every large-range sequence against the path length; open markers are Spatial Arena. twice as accurate on the upright front camera as on the rolled side cameras: the side-to-front ratio of the AbsRel has median of 2.14 for VGGT-Ω, 2.16 for MoGe-3, and 2.28 for UniDepthV2, and it exceeds one in 18 or 19 of the 19 scenes. The error grows steadily with roll (Fig. 7(d)): for MoGe-3, from 9.8% below 15 to 22.1% at 4560 and 23.5% at 6090. On the upright front camera, VGGT-Ω reaches 8.4%, within 1.8 of its public error, whereas on the side cameras it reaches 16.218.0%. VGGT-Ω degrades least at large roll (16.8% at 6090, against 23.531.6% for MoGe-3, UniDepthV2, and DA3-G), which suggests that more diverse camera orientations in training reduce this dependence. (cid:17) Key finding Current models rely on gravity-aligned prior, with the ground at the bottom and the sky at the top of the image, that they acquire from upright training images; they have not learned to predict depth independently of in-plane rotation. The wide depth range is second cause. Binning the pixels of all 1,688 images by ground-truth depth shows that the error is lowest between 1 and 5 (1119% for the six best models) and rises both below 1 (2535%) and beyond 20 (2026%; 3138% for Depth Pro and VGGT). Beyond 20 m, all ten models underestimate depth, by mean log error of 0.18 (UniDepthV2) to 0.62 (DUSt3R) and 1.03 (SenseNova-Vision), i.e., they compress distant structure towards the camera. Because our alignment fits one scale and shift per image, it cannot undo such non-linear compression, and the error remains in the score. The compression is consistent with training sets whose dense depth is either indoor (a few meters) or capped at the range of 14 SpatialArena: Where Do Geometric Foundation Models Stand? driving LiDAR, so that near and far structure rarely appear in one training image. (cid:17) Key finding Depth models are calibrated to the narrow depth range of their training images: they are accurate at 15 but compress distant structure towards the camera, an error that no per-image scale and shift can remove. Why models fail on Spatial Arena: VideoDepth. video provides temporal context and, to the multi-view models, parallax, which could in principle resolve both failures. We test this on the 15 Spatial Arena clips (Fig. 8(a,b)). It does not. Binning the pixels by depth (every fourth frame, five models) reproduces the MonoDepth profile: the error of VGGT-Ω is 8.5% at 25 and rises to 25.1% below 1 and 17.0% beyond 20 m, and beyond 20 m, all five models underestimate depth, by mean log error of 0.14 (VGGT-Ω) to 0.59 (ChronoDepth). ChronoDepth also overestimates depth below 1 (+0.47); it flattens the whole depth range, which explains its 88.6% error at close range and its failure on the far opening of the corridor in Fig. 17(a). The camera dependence persists as well: all 15 models that cover every clip are less accurate on the nine side-camera clips than on the six front-camera clips, by 1.12.7 (median 1.7). The gap is smallest for DVD (1.1) and SenseNova-Vision (1.3), but only because they are inaccurate already on the front clips (35.0% and 40.2%, against 8.3% for VGGT-Ω). Only one walk contributes clips from both kinds of camera, so scene content adds to this gap, but its size and consistency across models agree with the MonoDepth analysis. The multi-view models suffer less from the compression than the video diffusion model (log error 0.14 to 0.45 against 0.59), which indicates that parallax helps, but not enough to recover distant structure. (cid:17) Key finding Temporal context does not remove either failure. Video models inherit the gravity prior and the depth compression of single-image models; parallax from multi-view models reduces the compression but does not remove it, and diffusion-based video depth flattens the whole depth range. Why models fail on Spatial Arena: SfM. Each Spatial Arena SfM scene mixes the upright front camera with the two rolled side cameras, whose views point in different directions and overlap little with each other. We therefore split the image pairs of the seven scenes by camera and compute the AUC@5 separately for each kind of pair (eight models, Fig. 8(c)). For every model, pairs of two front images are the most accurate and pairs from the two different side cameras the least accurate, by 1.67.4 (VGGT-Ω: 0.250 against 0.124; MapAnything: 0.071 against 0.010). Pairs from the same side camera, which share the roll but view similar content, lie in between. Two factors therefore compound: the roll of the side cameras lowers accuracy even when the views overlap, and the small overlap between differently oriented cameras lowers it further. third factor limits all pairs alike. The models process the 16001296 images at width of 504518 pixels (Tab. 29), so that one 14-pixel patch spans about 2.5 of the 90 field of view, half of the 5 threshold. The coarse loop is therefore recovered (median AUC@30 0.404), but fine accuracy is not (median AUC@5 0.043). Finally, because the models regress poses directly from image tokens, without the geometric verification by which COLMAP rejects matches between similar-looking but distinct places, repeated structure produces spurious jumps  (Fig. 25)  . (cid:17) Key finding Feed-forward pose estimation is reliable only for upright views that overlap strongly. Rolled views, small overlap between differently oriented cameras, working resolution of about 2.5 per token, and the absence of geometric verification together explain the scattered cameras and spurious jumps on Spatial Arena. Why models fail on Spatial Arena: SLAM. On the short range, the 14 feed-forward models that drift by at most 18.2% on 7-Scenes drift by 42221% on Spatial Arena, although the sequences have similar number of input frames (325 on median). The difference lies in the camera motion: the short Spatial Arena sequences cover 179 m, so the camera moves 0.55 between input frames, against 0.10 on 7-Scenes and 0.05 on TUM RGB-D. Over all short-range sequences of all datasets, the drift of every model except Pi-Long and ABot-Recon increases with this motion (Fig. 8(d); median ρ = 0.48 over the feed-forward models). Below 15 SpatialArena: Where Do Geometric Foundation Models Stand? 0.1 per frame, their median drift is 1121%; at 0.3 or more, which only Spatial Arena and Oxford Spires reach, it is 33268%. Large motion reduces the overlap between consecutive frames and produces baselines outside the range of the video clips on which these models are typically trained, so consecutive poses are estimated from little shared content, and their errors accumulate. Only Pi-Long and ABot-Recon behave in the opposite way: they drift less on such sequences (10.4% and 11.0%; ρ = 0.37 and 0.59). The camera roll plays no role here, since five of the eight Spatial Arena SLAM sequences use the front camera. The long range separates the number of frames from the length of the walk. On the public datasets, it consists only of indoor sequences (7-Scenes and TUM RGB-D) whose camera paths are 610 long, and it feeds the same 7-Scenes recordings as the short range at smaller stride, i.e., with about three times as many frames over the same path. The additional frames change nothing: for seven of the nine feed-forward models that run both Spatial Arena ranges, the median drift on the long 7-Scenes range is within 0.951.02 of the short-range drift (CUT3R and Fast3R are the exceptions), e.g., 11.7% against 12.2% for VGGT-Ω. The two long Spatial Arena walks cover 254 and 294 in 1,001 and 1,148 frames (Fig. 8(e)). Although the camera moves less per frame than on the short Spatial Arena range (0.25 against 0.55 m), the median drift of the feed-forward models doubles (median 1.98), to 96466% (VGGT-Ω, 168%; π3-X, 144%), against 7123% on the public long range. Errors thus accumulate along the path once the walk extends far beyond the local context of the model, which the indoor sequences of the public long range never test. The long-sequence systems split into two groups. Pi-Long (17.9%), ABot-Recon (36.1%), LoGeR (43.6%), and VGGT-Long (53.0%) keep the drift low, whereas ZipMap (352%) and R3 (246%) drift as much as the feed-forward models. On the large range, where the public datasets do contain outdoor paths (median 1.7 km on KITTI Odometry and 1.6 km on VBR), the same split appears within systems (Fig. 8(f)): the drift of LoGeR and LingBot-Map grows with the path length (ρ = 0.67 and 0.51 over all large-range sequences), whereas that of Pi-Long and ABot-Recon does not (ρ = 0.04 and 0.42), and Pi-Long drifts by 19.7% on Spatial Arena and 16.9% on the public large range. (cid:17) Key finding Drift grows with the camera motion between frames and, once the walk leaves the local context of the model, with the length of the walk; the number of frames alone does not matter. Feed-forward models track well only on short, slow, indoor paths. Only long-sequence systems that bound the error per chunk, most consistently Pi-Long, keep the drift low on long outdoor walks, which Spatial Arena provides on every range. Why models fail on Spatial Arena: MVRecon. MVRecon combines the two previous mechanisms. It aligns the predicted cameras to the ground truth, recovers the scale from the camera centers, and fuses the depth maps with it. Depth that is compressed at long range then places distant surfaces too close to the cameras, and pose errors among the rolled side views misplace whole depth maps; both move points beyond the 25 cm threshold. This is consistent with the reconstructions of Figs. 19 and 20, whose shapes are recognizable but whose scale and placement are wrong. We did not measure the error of the fused points per distance, so this explanation rests on the depth and pose analyses above rather than on direct measurement. (cid:17) Key finding across tasks The failures on Spatial Arena trace to three properties that the public benchmarks lack: rolled views, which break the gravity prior of depth and pose models; wide depth range within one image, which every model compresses at long range; and large camera motion between frames over long walks, along which feed-forward models accumulate drift. None of these properties depends on the scale of scene alone. Across data: rankings change. Because these failure modes affect models to different degrees, public rankings transfer only partly. The rank correlation between public and Spatial Arena results is high for depth (ρ = 0.730.91) and SfM (0.870.88), low for MVRecon (0.40), and absent for short-range SLAM (0.07), and the leader changes in every task except VideoDepth. In MonoDepth, the three most accurate public models are monocular specialists (MoGe-3, MoGe-2, MoGe), whereas on Spatial Arena the three most accurate are 16 SpatialArena: Where Do Geometric Foundation Models Stand? 3D/4D models (VGGT-Ω, AMB3R, π3-X); in MVRecon, IGGT ranks 13th of 16 on the public datasets (F-score 0.348) but first on Spatial Arena (0.197), whereas the public leader DA3-G falls to eighth (0.122); in SfM, DA3-G falls from second to ninth in AUC@5; and in short-range SLAM, VGGT-Ω has the lowest public drift (12.7%) but drifts by 66.2% on Spatial Arena. model that is selected on public benchmarks is therefore not necessarily the best choice for large, uncontrolled scenes. Across inputs. Additional inputs should not degrade model, but the rgbc and rgbd tracks show that for current models they sometimes do (Tabs. 18 and 19). Ground-truth cameras help weaker reconstructions: the MVRecon F-score of MapAnything increases from 0.264 to 0.746 on ETH3D. In contrast, DA3-NGL degrades severely when conditioned on cameras (mean F-score 0.667 to 0.222; 0.870 to 0.086 on HiRoom), and depth priors halve the SfM AUC@5 of π3-X on DTU (0.743 to 0.336) and raise its MVRecon Acc on 7-Scenes from 0.24 to 20.5 m. prior that conflicts with the image evidence, in convention, scale, or density, is evidently not reconciled with it but followed. This points to conditioning that was trained on clean, consistent priors and is not robust to the conventions and noise of real ones.

sections.title: 5.2 Robustness
sections.content: Failure cases on Spatial Arena: depth. The qualitative results show the failures analyzed in Sec. 5.1. On the Spatial Arena frame of Fig. 11, VGGT-Ω has an AbsRel of 13.2% and VGGT of 35.6%, although the two models differ by only 1.4 points on the public datasets. In VideoDepth  (Fig. 17)  , ChronoDepth misses the far opening of corridor (0.171, against 0.044 for Déjà View and π3-X), an instance of the compressed far range. On close-up of nearly planar museum surface, every model fails to some degree (0.1170.375), and VGGT-Ω and DA3-NGL, first and third on the public VideoDepth datasets, are among the least accurate. Such view contains no horizon, ground plane, or familiar object that would anchor learned layout prior. The VLMs fail even on the coarse layout: in the library corridor  (Fig. 14)  , Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra return nearly planar depth (0.399 and 0.392). Failure cases on Spatial Arena: reconstruction and poses. In MVRecon, no model exceeds an F-score of 0.35 on the scenes of Fig. 19, and on the roof  (Fig. 20)  , most models recover the shape but at the wrong scale and position. In SfM, all models recover the overall loop around the Dugald Stewart Monument  (Fig. 24)  , but their cameras scatter around it (best AUC@5 0.230, Déjà View; MapAnything 0.005). Around the St Giles statue  (Fig. 25)  , whose sides look alike, DA3-NGL and VGGT add spurious jumps across the loop. These are the effects of camera roll, small overlap, low working resolution, and missing geometric verification analyzed in Sec. 5.1. Failure cases on Spatial Arena: long recordings. The 14 feed-forward models that drift by at most 18.2% on the short 7-Scenes sequences drift by 42221% on those of Spatial Arena. As analyzed in Sec. 5.1, the cause is the camera motion between frames. On the large range (Fig. 21b), only Pi-Long keeps the drift below 50% (27.0%, ATE 13.1 m); the other systems drift by 51155% or collapse onto small region, and VGGT-SLAM returns poses for only 10% of the frames. Pi-Long chunks the input of strong feed-forward model and aligns overlapping chunks, which bounds both memory and the error per chunk. Unlike the other tasks, the large range of Spatial Arena is about as difficult as the public long recordings (median drift 80.1% against 83.4%); for SLAM, Spatial Arena adds most on the short and long ranges. Input length and memory. On the public datasets, most failures stem from input length rather than from prediction errors. Global attention over all frames requires memory that grows quadratically with the number of tokens, and pairwise models must process number of pairs that grows quadratically with the number of frames. sections.title: 5.3 Accuracy
sections.content: Coarse versus fine accuracy. On the public datasets, coarse accuracy is close to saturation, but fine accuracy is not. The best δ1.25 is 98.299.5% on the Marigold suite, HAMMER, iBims-1, and AerialMetric, and the best SfM AUC@30 is 0.890.98 on DTU, ETH3D, HiRoom, IMC, and Tanks and Temples, whereas the best δ1.03 is only 70.782.1% and the median AUC@5 is 0.360.74. Fine thresholds also separate the models better: on HAMMER and iBims-1, the median model is within 2.1 points of the best δ1.25 but 1423 points behind the best δ1.03. We see two limits on fine accuracy. The models predict at fraction of the input resolution, and their training objectives are dominated by the coarse structure of scene, which δ1.25-level prediction already captures. On Spatial Arena, fine accuracy is the first to break, with best δ1.03 of 35.9% (Tab. 5). Drift and global consistency. Errors grow rapidly with trajectory length: the best short-range ATE is 1.0 cm on TUM and 4.0 cm on 7-Scenes, whereas the best large-range drift is 9.827% of the path length (Tab. 15). Low drift does not imply global consistency, nor does low ATE imply small local errors. ABotRecon has the lowest drift on KITTI, VBR, and the short Spatial Arena range, but on the large range about three times the ATE of Pi-Long on Oxford Spires and Spatial Arena (16.0 and 36.8 against 5.5 and 13.1 m), although it has the lowest ATE on VBR (16.5 m), while LingBot-Map shows the opposite pattern. Locally accurate tracking and globally consistent maps are thus different capabilities, and only Pi-Long ranks among the three best systems in both drift and ATE on every large-range dataset.

sections.title: 5.4 Strengths and weaknesses of the evaluated models
sections.content: Table 7 summarizes the strengths and weaknesses of each model family. We draw five conclusions from it. (1) Multi-view 3D/4D models are the strongest general-purpose geometric models today, but they are not yet reliable. They enter all five tasks, lead VideoDepth, MVRecon, and SfM, and are the most accurate single-image depth models on Spatial Arena, where VGGT-Ω is also the least sensitive to camera roll. Their weaknesses are long inputs, on which window-wise alignment accumulates drift (42221% even on short Spatial Arena sequences), fine pose accuracy, which their low working resolution and the absence of geometric verification limit, and priors, which they follow even when the priors conflict with the image. (2) Monocular specialists remain the most accurate single-image models on upright views of controlled scenes, but they depend on that setting. They have the lowest AbsRel on every public MonoDepth dataset, yet their error rises by 2.74.2 on Spatial Arena and more than doubles under strong camera roll, which indicates learned gravity prior rather than an understanding of geometry that is independent of orientation. (3) Dedicated video depth models have been overtaken. The best 3D/4D model is more accurate on every VideoDepth dataset, and on Spatial Arena the video depth models have 3.44.6 the error of VGGT-Ω; temporal smoothness without multi-view geometry does not resolve the depth of distant structure. (4) Long recordings require dedicated long-sequence machinery, and its robustness is the bottleneck. Only the long-sequence systems run the large range, and they also lead the short Spatial Arena range, on which the feed-forward models drift. Chunking strong feed-forward model with overlapping alignment, as Pi-Long does, is currently the most reliable design; the other systems fail through memory exhaustion, incomplete trajectories, or drift above 50%. (5) VLMs recover the coarse metric layout but are not yet geometric models. They improve fastest on MonoDepth and approach the median model on some public datasets, but on Spatial Arena their best AbsRel is 28.2% and their δ1.03 is at most 13.9%. We query the commercial VLMs at only 1616 points (Sec. D.3.2), so their scores bound only their coarse accuracy. Overall, no family combines breadth, fine accuracy, and robustness to viewpoint, depth range, and input length. The public benchmarks share the upright viewpoints, narrow depth ranges, and short inputs of the training data, and therefore do not expose these weaknesses; Spatial Arena does. 19 SpatialArena: Where Do Geometric Foundation Models Stand? sections.title: 5.5 Implications for future work
sections.content: These observations suggest six directions for the design and evaluation of geometric foundation models. 1. Remove the dependence on upright views. The error more than doubles under camera roll. Training with in-plane rotation and with views that look up or down, or conditioning on the gravity direction where device provides it, should close much of this gap; evaluation should include such views. 2. Cover near and far structure in one image. All models compress depth beyond 20 m. Training data in which near and far structure appear together, and losses that weight relative error uniformly over depth, address the failure that single scale and shift cannot correct. 3. Verify geometry and raise working resolution. Spurious jumps on repeated structure and the gap between AUC@30 and AUC@5 call for geometric consistency checks inside or after the network and for pose estimation at higher resolution. 4. Handle large motion, bound memory, and correct drift. Training sequences with large camera motion between frames should accompany the small-motion video clips that dominate current training data. SpatialArena: Where Do Geometric Foundation Models Stand? Models should run within bounded memory, through streaming, chunking, or compressed state, and correct accumulated scale drift, e.g., through loop closure or global optimization. 5. Detect failures and handle priors. Incomplete trajectories, constant predictions, and far outliers produce plausible-looking outputs; per-frame and per-point confidence is needed to expose them. Prior conditioning should be trained on noisy, sparse, and inconsistently scaled inputs, so that model given cameras or depth is never less accurate than without them. 6. Evaluate fine accuracy on uncontrolled data. δ1.25 and AUC@30 are saturated on most public datasets, whereas δ1.03 and AUC@5 on Spatial Arena still separate the models, under common robust alignment on audited test data.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented SpatialArena, an open arena that evaluates geometric foundation models on five tasks, 23 public datasets, and our Spatial Arena captures under one protocol, with robust and deterministic alignment of depth and trajectories, and with leaked test data excluded from the ranking. Evaluating 52 models shows that single-image depth is close to saturation on public benchmarks but not on large, uncontrolled scenes, that progress now comes from consistency across frames and views, where feed-forward 3D/4D models match or surpass the monocular specialists and overtake dedicated video depth models, and that visionlanguage models improve fastest on single-image depth but still lack metric precision. No model leads on every dataset, and long recordings remain out of reach for feed-forward models on their own. Limitations. We measure the effect of camera roll by comparing images, not by rotating them, so content that differs between front and side views, such as more sky and facades in the side views, contributes to the gap; the same-scene comparison and the monotonic trend with roll make roll the most likely main factor, but not the only one. The trends rest on one to three years of releases per model family and are indicative rather than forecasts. Several comparisons involve few models (four accept auxiliary inputs, eight run the large SLAM range), some models cover Spatial Arena only partially (marked ), and we evaluate the commercial VLMs only on MonoDepth and through 1616 query grid. We will keep the leaderboard open to new models and datasets.

sections.content: In Sec. A, we detail the datasets, the protocol of each task, and our data leakage audit. In Sec. B, we report the complete quantitative and qualitative results, including the scores on the public datasets alone (Sec. B.3). We define the metrics in Sec. sections.title: A Datasets and Protocol
sections.content: We list every dataset of SpatialArena with its scenes, images, ground truth, and input tracks in Tab. 8. Evaluation environment. We run all evaluations on cluster of NVIDIA H200 GPUs (141 GB of memory each) with 512 GB of host RAM per node. Each job runs one method on one GPU, so the memory limits that we report are those of single H200 and of the host RAM of its node. We run the commercial VLMs through their APIs (Sec. D.3.2). Frame selection and input resolution. To give all feed-forward models identical inputs, we cap each scene of VideoDepth, MVRecon, and SfM at 100 frames, following DA3-BENCH [55]; for Spatial Arena, we feed the VideoDepth clips whole and cap the MVRecon and SfM scenes at 300 frames. For larger scenes, we draw fixed-seed random subset in temporal order and process it in one forward pass, so that all predictions of scene share one coordinate frame. We run each method at its own native input resolution and map its outputs back to the source image, so we always compute the metrics at ground-truth resolution. We list the resolution, resizing, padding, and output masking of every model in every task in Sec. D.3.1. MonoDepth. We take NYUv2, KITTI (Eigen split), ETH3D, and DIODE from the Marigold suite [44]. Following the zero-shot suite of MoGe [92], we add HAMMER (indoor tabletop scenes with high-quality depth), iBims-1 (indoor scans with dense laser depth), and Spring (rendered film scenes with relative depth). We further add Synth4K (38402160 frames from five video games), AerialMetric (UAV viewpoints in three scenes), and 1,688 Spatial Arena images from 19 indoor and outdoor scenes. We treat each test set of the Marigold suite as one scene, and we use the frames and validity masks of MoGes zero-shot suite [92] for HAMMER, iBims-1, and Spring. Since Synth4K publishes no evaluation list, we keep half of the frames of each game with ground truth in (3, 150) m, spaced uniformly. AerialMetric covers controlled pitch, altitude, and field-of-view sweeps, oblique views, and online videos; we sample it in the same way and mask out moving objects. VideoDepth. Sintel has 23 synthetic, highly dynamic sequences; Bonn 26 indoor RGB-D sequences with moving people and objects; KITTI 13 driving sequences with projected LiDAR depth; DyCheck 12 casual handheld phone captures of people, pets, and objects in motion; and Spatial Arena 15 single-camera clips of 132 to 1,021 frames from seven walks. For DyCheck, we use the first camera of the evaluation release distributed by MegaSaM [53], with its depth maps at their native resolution. We pair the Bonn depth maps with RGB frames by nearest timestamp (within 0.25 s). In Spatial Arena, 26 frames failed our manual review of the ground truth; we keep them as model inputs but do not score them. MVRecon. For ScanNet++ and HiRoom, we follow the scene lists of DA3-BENCH [55]. We run the rgbd track only where the ground-truth depth is sparse or incomplete (7-Scenes, ETH3D, and DTU), so that the prior does not already contain the reference surface. Two ETH3D scenes (meadow and terrace) have no released reference surface; we leave them out, which leaves 11 ETH3D scenes. For each Spatial Arena scene, we feed method fixed-seed subset of 300 of its 363 to 1,806 images and use the LiDAR map as the reference, cropped to the points that some view sees in front of its dense depth, so that completeness does 28 SpatialArena: Where Do Geometric Foundation Models Stand? Table 8. Dataset checklist of SpatialArena. MonoDepth scores every image. VideoDepth, MVRecon, and SfM cap every scene at 100 evaluated frames (fixed-seed sampling, temporal order preserved), except on Spatial Arena, where we evaluate the VideoDepth clips whole and cap the MVRecon and SfM scenes at 300 frames. We feed the SLAM sequences whole at fixed stride; their #Evaluated lists the frames fed per range track (short / long, short / large, or short / long / large). For the public datasets, these are the same sequences at different strides; each Spatial Arena sequence runs in one track only, so its three numbers count disjoint sequences (3 / 2 / 3). Comparison of alignment choices. To measure how much the alignment alone changes score, we re-score identical MonoDepth predictions under six alignments: we fit in depth or in inverse depth and estimate the affine parameters by ℓ1 with fixed number of Adam steps (as in CUT3R and π3 [91, 95]), by least squares (as in Marigold [44]), or by our Huber IRLS. All six share the ground-truth-only pixel set and the metric computation, which is always in depth. We evaluate four models with different output parameterizations: two multi-view geometry models, VGGT-Ω [89] and DA3-G [55], which predict depth up to scale; Lotus-D [34], which predicts affine-invariant disparity; and Marigold v1.1 [44], which predicts affine-invariant depth. The study covers 15 MonoDepth subsets and 5,205 images (Tab. 21); we give per-subset results, including RMSE, in Sec. D.1.2. We make three observations. First, Huber IRLS is the best estimator in every one of the eight (model, space) combinations, for both AbsRel and δ1.25. Least squares is pulled by outlier pixels; in depth 53 SpatialArena: Where Do Geometric Foundation Models Stand? space it raises the AbsRel of VGGT-Ω and DA3-G by 5559% over Huber IRLS. The fixed-step ℓ1 fit is unreliable when the prediction is far from the ground-truth scale, as for the normalized outputs of Lotus-D and Marigold: its AbsRel reaches 0.82 for Lotus-D in depth space. Second, for the multi-view models the space of the fit hardly matters once the estimator is robust (AbsRel within 0.006, δ1.25 within 0.1 points). Third, for the relative-depth models the space decides the result: the AbsRel of Lotus-D nearly triples when we fit its disparity in depth space (0.264 against 0.096; δ1.25 of 64.4% against 90.0%), and Marigold v1.1 behaves in the opposite way, with an AbsRel twice as high in inverse depth (0.258 against 0.127; δ1.25 of 66.5% against 86.8%). An affine fit is therefore best suited to the space in which models output is affine-invariant. This motivates our default: Huber IRLS in the native output space that each model declares, which is the best alignment for Lotus-D and Marigold and, for VGGT-Ω and DA3-G, matches the best δ1.25 and is within 0.006 of the best AbsRel. We treat the space as property of the models output, declared once in the registry, not as per-dataset tuning choice. The real trajectories confirm our simulation results. Our estimator is exact under outliers and jumps, where evo understates the error by up to 2.6. It matches evo under noise. Among the RANSAC variants, ours absorbs the least extra error (ATE ratio 0.45, against 0.43 for evo). D.3 Model inputs and commercial VLM queries D.3.1 Input preprocessing Per-model preprocessing. We run each method at its own native input resolution and record this resolution profile with the results. Our adapters record the exact resize, padding, and crop applied to each image and invert them on the output: they return depth and confidence maps on the source pixel grid, mark border pixels that the model never saw as invalid, and export intrinsics that describe the source image. Where models own loader would crop image content, our adapter pads instead, wherever the model allows it. We list the result for every model in Tab. 29. We resize predictions that are not on the source grid bilinearly to the ground truth before scoring. In MonoDepth, we give each image to multi-view models as single-view input and to pairwise models as the pair (image, image). SLAM inputs. In SLAM, all methods see identical pixels. We write every sequence once at width of 504 pixels (36 patches of 14 px), close to the datasets own aspect ratio: 504378 for 7-Scenes, TUM RGB-D, and Oxford Spires, 504252 for VBR, 504154 for KITTI Odometry, and 504406 for Spatial Arena. We resize each frame to fit and zero-pad it by at most few pixels, never crop it, and map the ground-truth intrinsics and the rgbd priors in the same way. The methods keep these frames unrescaled: models that require square canvas pad them, models with 16-pixel patches crop border of at most 8 px, and for methods whose code fixes another size, we set it to the input size (Tab. 29). 59 SpatialArena: Where Do Geometric Foundation Models Stand? D.3.2 Querying commercial VLMs Claude Opus 5.5 [2], GPT-6 Astra [60], and Gemini 4 Argon [29] return depth only as text, and every request re-sends the whole image, so asking for one pixel per request would multiply the cost by the number of queried points. We therefore ask for whole grid of points in single request per image, through the OpenRouter API, on MonoDepth only. Query. We resize each image to long side of 1,024 pixels and send it twice as JPEG: the clean photo, and copy with 1616 grid of numbered red dots. The dots are spaced uniformly, with margin of half cell from the image border, and each carries its number, from 1 to 256 in row-major order, on white tag. We ask the following user message (no system prompt): The first image is photo. The second image is the same photo with 256 red dots, each labelled with number from 1 to 256; use the first image to see the scene the markers cover. For every dot, estimate the metric depth of the scene point under the dot centre: its distance from the camera along the cameras viewing (optical) axis, in meters. If dot lies on the sky or on anything effectively infinitely far away, answer "sky" instead of number. Give numeric estimate for every other dot even when unsure. Return the final answer as single JSON object mapping each dot number (as string) to its depth in meters (or "sky"), wrapped in <answer> </answer> tags, e.g. <answer>{"1": 2.4, "2": "sky", "3": 3.1, ...}</answer>. We query all three models with temperature 0, reasoning effort low (the reasoning text is not returned), and at most 8,192 output tokens, and only through providers that do not store or train on the prompts. Incomplete answers. Some answers stop after the first rows of dots. In this case, we send up to two follow-up messages in the same conversation that ask for exactly the missing dots, without re-sending the images: Your answer did not include dots <missing ranges, e.g. 97-256>. Give the metric depth (or "sky") for exactly these dots, estimated the same way and consistent with your previous estimates. Return one JSON object mapping each of these dot numbers (as string) to its depth, wrapped in <answer> </answer> tags. The follow-ups ask for the rest of the answer rather than re-sampling it, and we stop as soon as one adds no new dot. From answers to dense depth map. We clamp each answered depth to the depth range declared for the scene, so that, e.g., sky point answered at thousands of meters does not spread into its neighbors. We fill grid cells answered sky or left unparsed from their answered 8-neighbors with the mean log depth, from the nearest answers inward; single scene-median value per gap would leave flat blocks. We then upsample the 1616 grid bilinearly to the resized image and invert the resize, so that we score the map at ground-truth resolution with the per-image alignment of Sec. 3.3.1. An image without any parseable answer receives the scenes median depth, and we log it as an imputation; we score constant answer with the offset-only fit of Sec. D.1.1. Protocol selection. We chose this protocol on pilot of 14 images (two per MonoDepth dataset). Adding the clean photo and the sky answer lowered the aligned AbsRel by about 9% compared to single marked image with an 88 grid, and the 1616 grid lowered it little further. Neither an RGB-guided joint bilateral fill, second request for extra dots around depth edges, nor system prompt that frames the task for depth expert improved the aligned scores, so we use none of them. Cost. We record the billed cost of every request with its answer. Running the full MonoDepth suite, including the pilot and the follow-up requests, cost $510 for Claude Opus 5.5 (11,820 requests), $1,122 for GPT-6 Astra (11,804), and $364 for Gemini 4 Argon (11,706), $1,996 in total (OpenRouter prices of November 2026), i.e., about 4.3, 9.5, and 3.1 US cents per request.
